intro: Chaliapin and Keneman’s arrangement turns the Russian folk song into a bass solo with orchestra. This 1922 acoustic side, conducted by George W. Byng, precedes Chaliapin’s electrical remake by five years.
question: How does a solo bass give a repeated folk-song phrase direction?

cues.title: Folk song as bass solo
cues.text: The Victrola label credits Chaliapin and Keneman’s arrangement for bass with orchestra. Follow how the solo line carries the repeated song forward; this is a concert arrangement, not a field recording of a group at work.
cues.evidence: The digitised label and DAHR identify the arrangers and forces: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/2000007686. No verse or vocal entrance is assigned to this time.

cues.title: A gradual recorded rise
cues.text: Across the opening, the recorded level grows in stages. Listen for how the bass sustains the line through that growth rather than equating a stronger sound with a faster pulse.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/volga-boatmen-chaliapin-1922.txt: level rises from −26.6 dB at 0:05 to −14.6 at 0:35 and −11.0 at 0:50. These are within-transfer relative levels.

cues.title: Across the first crest
cues.text: This passage reaches an early crest and then draws back. Compare its phrase lengths with the 1927 remake; different orchestral balance and surface noise need not signify a different vocal intention.
cues.evidence: The report gives strong boundaries at 0:52 and 1:04, a high-level window at 0:55 and a drop at 1:05. The map follows the surrounding phrase, not individual words.

cues.title: Another broad rise
cues.text: A later swell carries the song onwards before another retreat. Attend to the bass line’s continuity across the crest and to what remains of the accompaniment beneath it.
cues.evidence: The report’s highest five-second window is 1:35, with high level continuing at 1:40 and a drop at 1:45. No particular syllable, register change or orchestral entrance is claimed.

cues.title: Repeated harmony needs caution
cues.text: The automatic comparison becomes locally uncertain through this stretch: repeated harmony can match more than one place. Compare the larger phrase by ear, not the apparent surge or stall in the timing curve.
cues.evidence: Inspection of the automatic path shows a plateau at reference 121–126 seconds and a compensating jump near 137–138 seconds, despite high chroma similarity. Local speed estimates around 2:00–2:25 should not be interpreted musically.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Before the final withdrawal
cues.text: The song passes through a final sustained high-level stretch before receding. Listen for the whole contour rather than assuming that the last large sound must be the ending.
cues.evidence: The report lists 2:20 and 2:25 among the loudest windows, followed by a fall at 2:30 and a boundary at 2:34. This is an envelope observation, not a verse label.

cues.title: Music and surface noise
cues.text: The closing span grows quieter until disc noise becomes more prominent. Follow the retreat of the musical line, and avoid reading the persistent hiss as continued orchestral sound.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −20.1 dB at 2:35 towards −28.6 at 3:00 while measured brightness rises. The alignment stops at 180 seconds rather than including the final noisy tail.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Russian folk song arranged by Fyodor Chaliapin and Fyodor Keneman; bass and orchestra
fields.note: The label spells the second arranger Koenemann. The arrangement, not an anonymous unarranged folk performance, is heard.
